Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verses 1–3:

﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾ meaning: when the Resurrection takes place. Al-Waqi'a (the Inevitable Event) is one of the names of the Resurrection, indicating its terror, like al-Tamma (the Overwhelming Calamity) and al-Sakha (the Deafening Blast). It is also said: ﴿al-Waqi'a﴾ means the Cry, which is the blast in the Trumpet. ﴿There is no denying its occurrence﴾ this may bear three interpretations. First: that al-Kadhiba is a verbal noun, like al-'Afiya, and the meaning is that there is no lying about it and no repelling it. Second: that kadhiba is an adjective of a omitted noun, as if he said: there is no soul (or state) that is lying, meaning it is certain to occur without doubt, and this meaning is close to the first. Third: that the implied phrase is: there is no soul that denies it, meaning no denial in rejecting the resurrection, because every soul will believe at that time. ﴿Abasing [some], exalting [others]﴾ the implied phrase is: it is abasing and exalting. The passage should be paused upon before it to clarify the meaning. The meaning of abasing and exalting is that it abases peoples to the Fire and exalts peoples to the Garden. It is also said that this is an expression of its terror, because the heaven will be split, the earth will shake and quake, and the mountains will be scattered, so it is as if it abases some of these bodies and exalts others.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verses 4–6:

﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾: i.e., it is quaked and moved with a severe motion. Here "idha" (when) is a substitute (badal) for the first "idha" (in the verse "When the Event occurs"), and it is possible that the governing element (al-'amil) in it is "khafidah rafi'ah" (abasing, elevating).

﴿And the mountains are crumbled, crumbling﴾: i.e., they are pulverized. It is also said: they are set in motion.

﴿And they become scattered dust, dispersed﴾: "al-haba'" (fine dust) is what flies about in the air as fine particles, and it is hardly seen except in sunlight when it enters through a window (kuwwa); this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: it is what flies from the hooves of beasts of dust. It is also said: it is what flies from sparks of fire, and when it is extinguished, nothing is found of it. And "al-munbath" means dispersed.

ۣ﴿And you will be divided into three categories﴾. This is addressed to all people, because on the Day of Resurrection they will be divided into these three categories: the foremost (al-sabiqun), the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), and the companions of the left (ashab al-shimal). As for the foremost, they are the people of the highest ranks in Paradise; as for the companions of the right, they are the rest of the people of Paradise; and as for the companions of the left, they are the people of the Fire. ﴿So the companions of the right — how blessed are the companions of the right!﴾ This is the beginning of a statement that carries the meaning of glorification, like your saying: "Zayd, what a Zayd!" The word al-maymanah may be derived from al-yaman, which is the opposite of ill omen, and al-mash'amah would then be derived from ill omen (al-shu'm). Or al-maymanah may refer to the side of the right, and al-mash'amah to the side of the left. The "ill-omened hand" is the left hand, because the Arabs associate good with the right and evil with the left. Or it may be because the people of Paradise are brought toward the right, and the people of the Fire are brought toward the left. Or it may refer to those who receive their book in the right hand or in the left. ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾: the first is the subject (mubtada') and the second is its predicate, in a manner of glorification, like your saying: "You are you," or with the meaning that those who are foremost in obedience to God are the foremost to Paradise. It has been said that the second "al-sabiqun" is an attribute (sifah) of the first or an emphasis (ta'kid), and the predicate is ﴿Those are the ones brought near﴾. The more preferred view is that the second is the predicate of the first, because it corresponds to His saying: ﴿So the companions of the right — how blessed are the companions of the right!﴾ and ﴿And the companions of the left — how wretched are the companions of the left!﴾. On this basis one pauses at the second "al-sabiqun" and begins with what follows.

﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples, and a few from the later ones.﴾ The *thullah* is a group of people. The meaning is that the foremost (*al-sabiqun*) from the earlier generations are more numerous than the foremost from the later generations. The earlier ones are the first of this *ummah* (community), and the later ones are the latter part of this *ummah*. The evidence for this is what is narrated, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The two groups are in my *ummah*." This is because the early generation of this *ummah* is better than those who came after them, so the foremost among the righteous predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*) were many, and then they became few. This is supported by his (ﷺ) saying: "The best of generations is my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them."

It has also been said that the two groups are in the community of every prophet, so the foremost in every community are more numerous at its beginning and fewer at its end. It has also been said that the earlier ones are those who came before this *ummah*, and the later ones are this *ummah*. This implies that the foremost of the earlier nations are more numerous than the foremost of this *ummah*, and this is far-fetched. It has also been said that by the foremost are meant the prophets, because they were more numerous in the earliest times than at the latest.

﴿On couches interlaced,﴾ the *surur* is the plural of *sarir* (couch), and *mawdunah* means woven, and it has been said it means interlaced with pearls and rubies. It has also been said it means continuous, with some of them drawn close to others.

﴿Reclining face to face.﴾ That is, the faces of some of them are turned toward others.

﴿Youths who remain ever young.﴾ The *wildan* are young servants, and *mukhalladun* means those who do not die. It has also been said it means those adorned with earrings of *khaladat*, a kind of earring, but the first view is more evident.

﴿With goblets and pitchers,﴾ the *akwab* is the plural of *kub*, which is a vessel without a handle or spout by which one holds it, and the *abariq* is the plural of *ibriq*, which is a vessel that has a spout or a handle by which one holds it.

﴿And a cup from a flowing spring.﴾ It is mentioned in Surat al-Saffat (37:45).

﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples, and a few from the later ones.﴾ The *thullah* is a group of people. The meaning is that the foremost (*al-sabiqun*) from the earlier generations are more numerous than the foremost from the later generations. The earlier ones are the first of this *ummah* (community), and the later ones are the latter part of this *ummah*. The evidence for this is what is narrated, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The two groups are in my *ummah*." This is because the early generation of this *ummah* is better than those who came after them, so the foremost among the righteous predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*) were many, and then they became few. This is supported by his (ﷺ) saying: "The best of generations is my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them."

It has also been said that the two groups are in the community of every prophet, so the foremost in every community are more numerous at its beginning and fewer at its end. It has also been said that the earlier ones are those who came before this *ummah*, and the later ones are this *ummah*. This implies that the foremost of the earlier nations are more numerous than the foremost of this *ummah*, and this is far-fetched. It has also been said that by the foremost are meant the prophets, because they were more numerous in the earliest times than at the latest.

﴿On couches interlaced,﴾ the *surur* is the plural of *sarir* (couch), and *mawdunah* means woven, and it has been said it means interlaced with pearls and rubies. It has also been said it means continuous, with some of them drawn close to others.

﴿Reclining face to face.﴾ That is, the faces of some of them are turned toward others.

﴿Youths who remain ever young.﴾ The *wildan* are young servants, and *mukhalladun* means those who do not die. It has also been said it means those adorned with earrings of *khaladat*, a kind of earring, but the first view is more evident.

﴿They will not be affected by headache from it, nor will they be intoxicated﴾. That is, no headache will reach their heads, the headache that afflicts those who drink the wine of this world. ﴿And fruit of what they choose﴾. It is said: they choose whatever they wish because of its abundance. And it is said: it is chosen and pleasing.

﴿And [there are] wide-eyed, beautiful maidens﴾. We have already explained its meaning.

The reading with the nominative, ḥūrun, is based on the assumption of "there are in them ḥūr," or it is coordinated with the pronoun in muttakiʾīna (reclining), or with wildānun (youths).

Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her) asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this comparison, and he said: "Their clearness is like the clearness of the pearl within the shells, which no hand has touched."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verses 25–26:

﴿They hear therein no idle talk, nor any sin.﴾ Laghw (idle talk) is worthless speech, such as obscenity and the like. Ta'thim (sin) is a verbal noun meaning that no one there makes himself or anyone else sinful. ﴿Only the saying: "Peace, peace."﴾ Salaman (peace) is in the accusative either as a substitute (badal) for qilan (saying), or as a qualifier (sifah) of it, or as the object (maf'ul bihi) of qilan, since its meaning is qawlan (a statement). According to this reading, the meaning of salam is greeting (tahiyyah), and the sense is that they exchange greetings abundantly, so that they greet one another with peace after peace. It is also possible that its meaning is safety (salamah), in which case it is in the accusative by a hidden verb whose estimated form is: "Be safe (aslimu) in safety."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verse 34:

﴿And raised couches﴾. They are the beds. It has been related that the height of the bed among them is a distance of five hundred years. It was also said: they are the women, but this is far-fetched.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verses 35–38:

﴿Indeed, We have created them﴾ The pronoun refers to the women of Paradise, as the context of the speech requires, even though they have not been mentioned before. Rather, the mention of the couches (al-furush) came earlier, and it indicates the women. As for the one who said that the couches are the women, then the pronoun returns to them. It was also said that it returns to the Ḥūr al-ʿĪn (the wide-eyed maidens) mentioned before this, but that is far-fetched, for that [mention] is in the description of the gardens of the foremost (al-sābiqūn), while this is in the description of the gardens of the companions of the right (aṣḥāb al-yamīn). The meaning of creating the women is that Allah the Exalted creates them in Paradise as a different creation, in the utmost beauty, unlike in this world, where the old woman returns young and the ugly woman returns beautiful. ﴿So We have made them virgins, * loving (ʿurub), equal in age (atrāb)﴾ ʿUruban is the plural of ʿarūb, who is the one who shows affection to her husband by displaying her love for him. Ibn ʿAbbās described them as those who are passionately devoted (al-ʿawāshiq) to their husbands. It was also said that she is the one good in speech. ﴿Equal in age * for the companions of the right﴾ That is, they are of equal age with their husbands. It was narrated that they will be in the age of the sons of thirty-three years. The phrase "for the companions of the right" is connected to His words ﴿We have created them﴾ according to what al-Zamakhsharī said. It is also possible that it is connected to atrāban (equal in age), and this is what the meaning requires: equal in age to their husbands.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verses 58–62:

﴿Have you considered that which you emit?﴾ This verse and what follows contain the establishment of proofs for the Oneness (of God) and for the Resurrection, and they also contain a warning and an enumeration of blessings. The meaning of "tumnūn" (تمنون) is: you eject the semen (al-manī).

﴿Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?﴾ This is a question that demands that they answer it by saying that God is the Creator, there is no god but Him.

﴿We have decreed death among you﴾, meaning We made it determined by known terms and lifespans, some long, some short, and some intermediate.

﴿And We are not to be outdone, that We may replace your likenesses and bring you into being in what you do not know.﴾ "Masbūq" (مسبوق) (one who is outdone) is the one who is overcome, such that he is unable to prevail over it. "Nubaddila amthālakum" (نُّبَدِّلَ أَمْثَالَكُمْ) means: We destroy you and substitute other people in your place. It was also said: We transform you into apes and swine. "Wa nunshi'akum" (وَنُنشِئَكُمْ) means: We resurrect you after your destruction. "Fī mā lā ta'lamūn" (فِي مَا لاَ تَعْلَمُونَ) means: We bring you into a form that you do not know, in a manner your intellects cannot reach to comprehend. So the meaning of the verse is that God is able to destroy them and able to resurrect them, and in it is both a threat and an argument for the Resurrection.

﴿Why then do you not remember?﴾ This is an exhortation to remembrance and to inferring the afterlife creation from the first creation. In this is evidence for the validity of analogical reasoning (qiyās).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verse 64–67:

﴿Do you then cultivate it, or are We the Cultivators?﴾ The meaning of "cultivation" (zir'ah) here is causing what is sown to sprout and bringing its creation to completion, because this is something God alone has exclusive control over and no one else can claim. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "None of you should say 'I have cultivated (zara'tu),' but let him say 'I have tilled (harathtu).'" The meaning of "tilling" (harth) is turning over the soil and casting the seed into it, and this may also be called zar' (cultivation), as in His words: ﴿It pleases the cultivators (zurra')﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. ﴿If We willed, We would make it into debris, and you would be left wondering (tafakkahun)﴾. "Hutam" (debris) is that which is dry and crumbled; it was also said that it means chaff without grain. ﴿Left wondering (tafakkahun)﴾ means: you would be made to abandon fruit (fakiha), which is joy. It is said: "a man is fakih" when he is joyful and open-hearted. It is also said: "tafakkaha" when joy has departed from him and he becomes sorrowful, because the form tafa''ala comes to denote the removal of a thing, as in the expressions "taharraja" and "ta'aththam" when hardship or sin has been removed from him. So the meaning is: you would become grieved over the crop if God made it debris. Some have expressed "tafakkahun" as meaning: you would lament, and it was said: you would regret, and it was said: you would marvel. These meanings are close, and the basic sense is what we have mentioned. ﴿Indeed we are laden with debt (mughramun). * Nay, we are deprived (mahrumun).﴾ Its implied sense is: you would say that if God had made your crop into debris. "Mughram" means one who is tormented, because gharam is the most severe punishment; it may also be from ghurm, meaning burdened by what we have spent in outlay on the crop. "Mahrum" is one whom God has deprived of good.

The first, which Ibn Abbas said, is that they are the stars of the Qur'an, when it was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ). The stars and their locations are their setting places and their falling places. It was also said: their positions in the sky. And it was said: their dispersal on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew.﴾ This is a parenthetical sentence (*jumla i'tiradiyya*) between the oath and its answer. His saying ﴿if you only knew﴾ is a parenthesis between the described noun and its description, so it is a parenthesis within a parenthesis. The purpose of this is to glorify the thing sworn by, which is ﴿the locations of the stars﴾. The answer to the oath is: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾. The pronoun refers back to the Qur'an because the meaning requires it, or because it is mentioned according to the view of the one who said that the locations of the stars are the revelation of the Qur'an. ﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾, meaning protected. The intended "Book well-guarded" is the codices (*masahif*) in which the Qur'an was written, or the pages of the Qur'an that are in the hands of the angels, peace be upon them.

﴿None touches it except the purified.﴾ The pronoun refers to the well-guarded Book. It may also refer to the Qur'an mentioned before it, but this is weak for two reasons. The first: touching the Book is literal, while touching the Qur'an is figurative, and the literal is preferable to the figurative. The second: the Book is closer, and the pronoun refers to the closest mentioned noun. If we say it refers to the well-guarded Book, then if the well-guarded Book is the pages in the hands of the angels, the "purified" are the angels, because they are purified from sins and defects, and the verse is a statement that none touches it except them, not others. If we say the well-guarded Book is the pages in the hands of people, then "the purified" may mean the Muslims, because they are purified from disbelief, or it may mean those purified from the major ritual impurity (*hadath akbar*), which is sexual impurity (*janaba*) or menstruation, so purification in this case is by bathing (*ghusl*), or those purified from the minor ritual impurity (*hadath asghar*), so purification in this case is by ablution (*wudu'*). It may also be that His saying ﴿none touches it﴾ is a statement or a prohibition. Some people have denied that it is a prohibition and said: if it were a prohibition, it would have been with a fatha on the sin (i.e., *yamassahu* rather than *yamussahu*). But the scholars (*al-muhaqqiqun*) said: the prohibition is valid even with a damma on the sin, because when a doubled verb is in the jussive mood, or is joined to a masculine singular pronoun, it takes a damma when two consonants meet, to match the vowel of the pronoun. If we take it as a statement, it may be intended as a simple statement, or it may be a statement with the meaning of a prohibition. If it is a simple statement, the meaning is: it is not appropriate that anyone touch it except the purified, meaning this is its right, even if something contrary to this occurs.

The jurists differed concerning who is permitted to touch the mushaf, according to the possibilities in the verse. They agreed that a disbeliever may not touch it, because if "the purified" means the Muslims, then the disbeliever is not purified; and if it means purification from ritual impurity, then Islam is still required in addition to that. As for ritual impurity, there are three views. The first: it is not permitted for one in sexual impurity, nor for a menstruating woman, nor for one with a minor ritual impurity to touch it. This is the view of Malik and his companions, and they also prohibited carrying it by its strap or cushion. Their proof is the verse, interpreting "the purified" as purification from both major and minor ritual impurity. Malik used the verse as evidence for this matter in the *Muwatta'*. Among their proofs also is the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Amr ibn Hazm: "That none touches the Qur'an except one who is pure." The second: it is permitted for one in sexual impurity, a menstruating woman, and one with a minor ritual impurity to touch it. This is the position of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the Zahiriyya (the literalist school). They interpreted "the purified" as the Muslims and the angels, or they made "none touches it" a mere statement. The third view: it is permitted to touch it with a minor ritual impurity but not a major one. Malik granted a concession for teachers and children to touch it without ablution, because of hardship.

They differed concerning the recitation of the Qur'an by one in sexual impurity. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa prohibited it absolutely, while the Zahiriyya permitted it absolutely, and Malik permitted reciting a small amount of the verse. Concerning the recitation of the Qur'an from memory by a menstruating woman and one in postpartum bleeding (*nafsa*), there are two reports from Malik on this matter, and some distinguished between a little and a lot.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verse 81–82:

﴿Do you then deny this discourse?﴾ This is addressed to the disbelievers, and the discourse referred to is the Qur'an. "Mudhinun" (those who are lax, scornful, or indifferent) means mutahawwinun (negligent), and its origin is from al-mudahana (idhan), which is softness of side and agreement outwardly rather than inwardly. Ibn 'Abbas said its meaning is "those who deny" (mukadhdhibun). ﴿And you make your provision that you deny⁠—﴾ Ibn 'Atiyya said: The exegetes have agreed that the verse is a rebuke to those who said about rain that it fell by such-and-such a star (nawʼ, lunar mansion). The meaning is: you make the thanks for your provision into denial. So the word "shukr" (thanks) has been omitted, and the phrase becomes "that you deny." Ibn 'Abbas recited it in the same way, except that he read "tukadhdhibun" with a damma on the ta' and with shaddah, like the reading of the majority. ʻAli's reading was with a fatha on the ta' and a sukun on the kaf, from al-kadhib (lying), meaning: you lie in your saying, "The rain fell by such-and-such a star." In this sense is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Allah the Exalted says: In the morning some of My servants become believers in Me and disbelievers in the star, and some become disbelievers in Me and believers in the star. As for the one who says, 'We have been given rain by the grace of Allah and His mercy,' he is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the star. As for the one who says, 'We have been given rain by such-and-such a star and such-and-such a constellation,' he is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the star."

What is forbidden in this matter is to believe that the star has an influence on the rain. As for observing the customary patterns which Allah has established, there is no harm in it, due to his (ﷺ) saying: "When you see a cloud rising in the west and then you become pessimistic, that is a heavy rain." Umar said to al-'Abbas, while they were seeking rain: "How much of the nawʼ of the Pleiades remains?" Al-'Abbas said: "The scholars say that it appears on the horizon seven nights after its setting." Ibn al-Tayyib said: "Seven nights had not passed before they were given rain."

It was also said: the meaning of the verse is "you make the cause of your provision your denial of the Prophet (ﷺ)," for they used to say: "If we believe in him, Allah will deprive us of provision," like their saying: ﴿If we follow the guidance with you, we shall be snatched away from our land﴾ [al-Qasas: 57]. Allah rebuked them for that. The grammatical analysis of "anna-kum" according to this view is that it is the object of "taj'alun" with an omitted modifier, its estimated form being: "you make the cause of your provision the denial." It may also be an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), its estimated form being: "you make your provision obtained because you deny." As for the first view, the grammatical analysis of "annakum tukadhdhibun" is simply an object (maf'ul) and nothing else.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verses 83–85:

﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat﴾ "Why not" (lawla) here is a rebuke/reproach (ʿaraḍ). The pronoun in "reaches" (balaghat) refers to the soul (nafs), because the context of the speech requires that, and its reaching the throat is at the time of death. The verb that lawla is attached to is His saying ﴿you would return it﴾, meaning: "Why did you not return the soul at the time of death?" The meaning of the verse is an argument against mankind and a demonstration of their helplessness, for when death comes to one of them, they are unable to return his spirit to his body, and that is evidence that they are subjugated slaves. ﴿And you at that time are looking on﴾ This is an address to those present at the deceased's deathbed from his relatives and others, meaning: you look at him and you cannot do anything for him. ﴿And We are nearer to him than you﴾ It may mean the nearness of His Own Self, exalted is He, by His knowledge and His awareness, or the nearness of the angels who take the souls, in which case it is nearness of distance. ﴿But you do not see﴾ If by His saying "We are nearer" he means the angels, then His saying ﴿you do not see﴾ is seeing with the eye; and if he means Himself, exalted is He, then it is seeing with the heart.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verse 86–87:

﴿Then why not, if you are not to be judged, [why not] bring it back, if you are truthful?﴾ Here "lawla" (why not / if only) is a reproach, as in the first instance, and it is repeated for emphasis and clarification, so that the speech does not become long. The verb that "lawla" (the first and second) governs is His saying ﴿tarji'ūnahā﴾ (you bring it back), meaning: "Why do you not return the soul to the body when it has reached the throat, if you are not indebted (to be judged), nor subject to a Lord and overpowered? Then do that, if you are truthful in your disbelief." The arrangement of the speech is: "Why do you not bring back the soul when it reaches the throat, if you are not indebted? Then bring it back, if you are truthful."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verses 88–89:

﴿If he is of those brought near﴾. The pronoun in *kāna* (is) refers to the deceased. Here he repeats what he mentioned at the beginning of the surah about dividing people into three categories: the *sābiqūn* (foremost), the companions of the right, and the companions of the left. So "those brought near" here means the foremost mentioned there.

﴿Then rest and rayhān﴾. *Rawḥ* means rest (*istirāḥa*). It was also said that it means mercy. It was narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited *fa-rūḥun* with a *ḍamma* on the *rā'*, and its meaning is mercy. It was also said that it means eternity, that is, the enduring of the spirit. As for *rayḥān*, it was said to mean provision, it was said to mean rest, it was said to mean fragrance, and it was said to mean the well-known *rayḥān* (basil plant). In His saying ﴿rawḥun wa-rayḥān﴾ there is a kind of *tajnīs* (paronomasia, a wordplay on similar-sounding words).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verse 91:

﴿Peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾. The meaning of this, in general, is the salvation and felicity of the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin). The word "peace" (al-salam) here may mean either safety (al-salama) or greeting (al-tahiyya). The address in this may be either to the Prophet (ﷺ) or to one of the companions of the right. If it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), then "peace" means safety, and the meaning is: "Safety be yours, O Muhammad, from them", that is, you will see from them nothing but safety from punishment. If the address is to one of the companions of the right, then "peace" means greeting, and the meaning is: "Peace be upon you", that is, a greeting to you, O companion of the right, from your brethren, who are the companions of the right; that is, they greet you, like His saying ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 26]. Or it may mean safety, and the sense is: "Safety be yours, O companion of the right", and then His saying ﴿from the companions of the right﴾ is the predicate of an implied subject, whose estimate is: "You are from the companions of the right."

**Translation:**

﴿And as for if he is among the deniers, the astray﴾, meaning the disbelievers, who are the companions of the left and the companions of the left side (al-mash'ama). ﴿Then, a welcome of boiling water﴾. The *nuzul* (welcome, hospitality) is the first thing that is offered to a guest.

**Translation:**

﴿And as for if he is among the deniers, the astray﴾, meaning the disbelievers, who are the companions of the left and the companions of the left side (al-mash'ama). ﴿Then, a welcome of boiling water﴾. The *nuzul* (welcome, hospitality) is the first thing that is offered to a guest.

﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty.﴾ The reference is to what this surah contains of the conditions of created beings in the Hereafter. The phrase *ḥaqq al-yaqīn* means the established part of certainty. It has also been said that *al-ḥaq* and *al-yaqīn* have one meaning, so this is an *iḍāfa* (annexation, a construct phrase) of a thing to itself, like the phrase مسجد الجامع (*masjid al-jāmi'*, "the mosque of the congregation"). Ibn ʿAṭiyya preferred that it be like your saying, when you want to emphasise a matter, هذا يقين اليقين (*hādha yaqīn al-yaqīn*, "this is the certainty of certainty") or صواب الصواب (*ṣawāb al-ṣawāb*, "the correctness of correctness"), meaning that it is the ultimate limit of correctness.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 56, verse 96:

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Make it part of your bowing (ruku')." Then when the verse ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed, he said, peace be upon him: "Make it part of your prostration (sujud)." Therefore Malik and others recommended that one say in prostration "Subhana Rabbiya al-A'la" (Glory be to my Lord, the Most High), and in bowing "Subhana Rabbiya al-'Azim" (Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty). The Zahiriyya made it obligatory. It is also possible that the meaning is glorifying Allah by mentioning His names, where "the name" (ism) here is a generic term for the names, and "the Mighty" (al-'Azim) is an attribute of the Lord. Or the word "name" here refers to one specific name, and "the Mighty" is its attribute, as if He commanded him to glorify by the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam). This is supported and hinted at by the connection of Surah al-Hadid to it, for at its beginning there is glorification and a number of Allah's names and attributes. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Greatest Name of Allah, the Mighty, the Greatest, is present in six verses at the beginning of Surah al-Hadid, and it is narrated that supplication is answered when reciting them.
